Fix a refinement factor $M\in\mathbb N$ with $M\ge2$, a base scale $T>0$, and a finite level $L\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The geometric mesh widths are $h_\ell=T M^{-\ell}$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Let $P$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E|P|<\infty$, and for each $\ell$ let $P_\ell$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E[P_\ell^2]<\infty$.

At level $0$, set $\Delta_0=P_0$. At each level $\ell\ge1$, choose a joint law for a pair $(P_\ell^{\mathrm f},P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c})$ whose marginals are the laws of $P_\ell$ and $P_{\ell-1}$, respectively. Such a joint law is a coupling of the two levels. Define the correction $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^{\mathrm f}-P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c}$. This construction gives $\mathbb E\Delta_\ell=\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P_{\ell-1}$.

For each level choose a positive integer $N_\ell$ and take $\Delta_{\ell,1},\ldots,\Delta_{\ell,N_\ell}$ to be independent copies of $\Delta_\ell$. Require the complete sample blocks from distinct levels to be independent. Write $\bar\Delta_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_\ell}\Delta_{\ell,i}$. The finite-level multilevel Monte Carlo estimator is
$$\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\bar\Delta_\ell.$$
All corrections have finite second moments because each level approximation does. The shared randomness inside one fine/coarse pair is what can reduce the correction variance; the estimator still uses independent sample blocks across levels.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $E_1,\ldots,E_m$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space, where $m\ge1$. Write $b_j=\mathbb E E_j$. Then
$$\mathbb E\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_j\right)^2\right]=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}b_j\right)^2+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Var}(E_j)+2\sum_{1\le j<k\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(E_j,E_k).$$
The correction to the sum of component variances is exactly $(\sum_j b_j)^2+2\sum_{j<k}\operatorname{Cov}(E_j,E_k)$. Thus the mean square equals the sum of component variances exactly when this combined correction is zero. In particular, if the total bias is zero, pairwise independence suffices.

derivations.claim: For each level $\ell$, the sample $\Delta_{\ell,1},\ldots,\Delta_{\ell,N_\ell}$ is IID by [F1] and square-integrable by [F2]. Applying [F3] to its sample mean gives $\mathbb E\bar\Delta_\ell=\mathbb E\Delta_\ell$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\bar\Delta_\ell)=V_\ell/N_\ell$.

The level-zero mean is $\mathbb E\Delta_0=\mathbb E P_0$. For $\ell\ge1$, the coupling marginals in [F1] give $\mathbb E\Delta_\ell=\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P_{\ell-1}$. Finite linearity [F4] and telescoping therefore yield $\mathbb E\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\mathbb E\bar\Delta_\ell=\mathbb E P_L$.

Set $\xi_\ell=\bar\Delta_\ell-\mathbb E\bar\Delta_\ell$. Each $\xi_\ell$ is square-integrable, centered, and measurable with respect to its own level sample block. The blocks are independent by [F1], so the $\xi_\ell$ are pairwise independent. Applying [F5] to their finite sum gives $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N})=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\operatorname{Var}(\bar\Delta_\ell)=\sum_{\ell=0}^L V_\ell/N_\ell$, using step 1.1.

The single error $E=\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}-\mathbb E P$ is square-integrable. By step 2.1 its mean is $\mathbb E P_L-\mathbb E P$, and by step 2.2 its variance is $\sum_{\ell=0}^L V_\ell/N_\ell$. The one-variable case of [F5] gives $\mathbb E[E^2]=\operatorname{Var}(E)+(\mathbb E E)^2$, which is the asserted MSE identity.

Put $v_\ell=C_vh_\ell^\beta$, $c_\ell=C_ch_\ell^{-1}$, and $S_L=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\sqrt{v_\ell c_\ell}$. Choose $N_\ell=\left\lceil2\epsilon^{-2}S_L\sqrt{\frac{v_\ell}{c_\ell}}\right\rceil,\qquad 0\le\ell\le L.$ Each $N_\ell$ is a positive integer. Since $V_\ell\le v_\ell$ and $N_\ell\ge2\epsilon^{-2}S_L\sqrt{v_\ell/c_\ell}$, [F3] gives $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N})\le\sum_{\ell=0}^L\frac{v_\ell}{N_\ell} \le\frac{\epsilon^2}{2S_L}\sum_{\ell=0}^L\sqrt{v_\ell c_\ell} =\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}.$ The bias bound from step 1.1 and the MSE identity [F3] imply the required MSE bound.

The ceiling inequality $\lceil x\rceil\le x+1$ and the per-sample work bound imply $\operatorname{Work}\le\sum_{\ell=0}^L N_\ell c_\ell \le2\epsilon^{-2}S_L^2+\sum_{\ell=0}^L c_\ell.$ Because $h_\ell=h_LM^{L-\ell}$, the geometric-series formula gives $\sum_{\ell=0}^L c_\ell=C_c\sum_{\ell=0}^Lh_\ell^{-1} \le\frac{C_c}{1-M^{-1}}h_L^{-1} =O(\epsilon^{-1/\alpha}).$

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on a complete filtered
probability space whose filtration is right-continuous and contains every
$P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in $\mathcal F_0$. Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$
be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are
independent of the current filtration. Let
$X_0$ be finite and $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$. Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius
matrix norm. Consider
the autonomous SDE
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t f(X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t g(X_s)\,dW_s, \qquad X_t\in\mathbb R^d,$$
where $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ are $C^1$. Assume that constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2, \qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2,$$
and
$$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2.$$
For each $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, let $Y^h$ be the continuous
Euler–Maruyama interpolation and $\bar Y^h$ its left-endpoint step process
from [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]. Assume
that an exact strong solution $X$ and these exact, step and continuous Euler
processes have uniformly bounded moments of every finite order on $[0,T]$:
for every $p\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^p+ \sup_{0<h\le1,\ T/h\in\mathbb N}\left( \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t^h|^p+ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|\bar Y_t^h|^p\right)<\infty.$$
Then a constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch.$$
In particular the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$.
The all-moment premise is part of this source contract; $X_0\in L^2$ alone
does not imply it.

Assume AC. Fix finite integers $d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, and $N\ge1$ such that
$h=T/N\le1$. Work on a filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite, $\mathcal F_0$-measurable,
and independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.
Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be $C^1$. Assume finite constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2,$$
$$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2.$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius
norm.

Set $t_k=kh$ and construct the grid approximation recursively by
$$Y_0=X_0,\qquad Y_{k+1}=Y_k+f(Y_k)h+g(Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}),\quad 0\le k<N.$$
The output also includes the left-endpoint step process
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N,$$
and the continuous interpolation
$$Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
The recursion makes the two interpolation formulas agree at every shared
endpoint. The finite recursion is defined pathwise: $C^1$ coefficients are
finite-valued, each $Y_k$ is finite almost surely by induction, and Brownian
paths are continuous. This algorithm defines no moment or convergence claim.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $M\ge2$ be an integer, $T>0$, and $h_\ell=T M^{-\ell}$. Let $P$ be an integrable real target. Suppose we are given an infinite compatible hierarchy: for every $\ell\ge0$ a square-integrable level approximation $P_\ell$, and for every $\ell\ge1$ a fixed coupling of the laws of $P_\ell$ and $P_{\ell-1}$. Define $\Delta_0=P_0$ and, under each coupling, $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^{\mathrm f}-P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c}$. For each finite $L$, use the first $L+1$ levels and their couplings, with independent sample blocks across levels, as in [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]]. Suppose there are constants $C_b,C_v,C_c>0$ and exponents $\alpha\ge\frac12$ and $\beta>0$ such that, for every $\ell\ge0$,
$$|\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P|\le C_b h_\ell^\alpha,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)\le C_v h_\ell^\beta,$$
and the work for one level-$\ell$ correction sample is at most $C_c h_\ell^{-1}$. For every sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, there are a finite level $L$ and positive integer sample counts $N_0,\ldots,N_L$ for which the estimator of [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]] satisfies
$$\mathbb E\left[(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}-\mathbb E P)^2\right]\le\epsilon^2$$
and its total work has the following upper bounds, with constants independent of $\epsilon$:
$$\begin{cases} O(\epsilon^{-2}),&\beta>1,\\ O\!\left(\epsilon^{-2}(\log\epsilon^{-1})^2\right),&\beta=1,\\ O\!\left(\epsilon^{-2-(1-\beta)/\alpha}\right),&0<\beta<1. \end{cases}$$
This is an upper bound under the three rate assumptions; it does not assert a matching lower bound or that the rates hold for a particular discretization.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A level-$\ell$ fine path has $T/h_\ell$ steps and its coarse partner has $T/(Mh_\ell)$ steps. For fixed $T,M$, dimension, and unit-cost coefficient and payoff evaluations, their total work is $O(h_\ell^{-1})$ for $\ell\ge1$. At level $0$, $Y_T^{h_0}$ has finite second moment by the all-moment premise, so the Lipschitz payoff gives $P_0\in L^2$; the single Euler path has finite work. Since $h_0=T$ is fixed, enlarge the constants so that the level-zero variance and work also satisfy the rate bounds required by [F4]. Applying [F4] with $\alpha=1/2$, $\beta=1$, and $\gamma=1$ gives the stated MSE and work bound. AC is inherited only from [A1]; no choice principle is used in the rate estimates.

the $M$ fine Brownian increments in that interval. Let $X_T$ be the common

The target mean is $\mathbb E P=\frac12+c/4$. Writing $\delta=\sqrt{h_\ell}$ and averaging over $S=\pm1$ gives $\mathbb E P_\ell=\tfrac12\bigl(\mathbb P(X\ge-\delta)+\mathbb P(X\ge\delta)\bigr)=\mathbb E P-\frac{c\delta^2}{4}.$ Thus $|\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P|=c h_\ell/4$, so the bias exponent is $\alpha=1$.

For $\ell\ge1$, put $\delta_f=\sqrt{h_\ell}$ and $\delta_c=\sqrt{h_{\ell-1}}=\sqrt M\,\delta_f$. The correction $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}$ is $+1$ when $S=-1$ and $\delta_f\le X<\delta_c$, is $-1$ when $S=+1$ and $-\delta_c\le X<-\delta_f$, and is zero otherwise. Fix a refinement factor $M\in\mathbb N$ with $M\ge2$, a base scale $T>0$, and a finite level $L\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The geometric mesh widths are $h_\ell=T M^{-\ell}$ for $0\le\ell\le L$. Let $P$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E|P|<\infty$, and for each $\ell$ let $P_\ell$ be a real random variable with $\mathbb E[P_\ell^2]<\infty$.

At level $0$, set $\Delta_0=P_0$. At each level $\ell\ge1$, choose a joint law for a pair $(P_\ell^{\mathrm f},P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c})$ whose marginals are the laws of $P_\ell$ and $P_{\ell-1}$, respectively. Such a joint law is a coupling of the two levels. Define the correction $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^{\mathrm f}-P_{\ell-1}^{\mathrm c}$. This construction gives $\mathbb E\Delta_\ell=\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E P_{\ell-1}$.

For each level choose a positive integer $N_\ell$ and take $\Delta_{\ell,1},\ldots,\Delta_{\ell,N_\ell}$ to be independent copies of $\Delta_\ell$. Require the complete sample blocks from distinct levels to be independent. Write $\bar\Delta_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_\ell}\Delta_{\ell,i}$. The finite-level multilevel Monte Carlo estimator is
$$\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\bar\Delta_\ell.$$
All corrections have finite second moments because each level approximation does. The shared randomness inside one fine/coarse pair is what can reduce the correction variance; the estimator still uses independent sample blocks across levels.

The target mean is zero, hence the MSE is exactly $1$ and cannot be made arbitrarily small. The missing hypothesis is convergence of $\mathbb E P_L$ to $\mathbb E P$; here the bias remains $1$.

Use the finite hierarchy and estimator of [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]]. Put $V_\ell=\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)$. Then
$$\mathbb E\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}=\mathbb E P_L,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N})=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\frac{V_\ell}{N_\ell},$$
and the mean square error for the target $\mathbb E P$ is exactly
$$\mathbb E\left[(\widehat\mu_{L,\mathbf N}-\mathbb E P)^2\right] =\sum_{\ell=0}^L\frac{V_\ell}{N_\ell}+(\mathbb E P_L-\mathbb E P)^2.$$

derivations.claim: Since $\mathbb E P_\ell=h_\ell$, the finest-level bias is $h_L$, so this hierarchy has bias order $\alpha=1$. For $\ell\ge1$, the independent centered Rademacher terms have variance $1+1=2$, hence $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)=2$ and no bound $O(h_\ell^\beta)$ holds for any $\beta>0$. The sample cost is exactly $h_\ell^{-1}$.

By [F2], the MSE is $h_L^2+\frac1{N_0}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^L\frac1{N_\ell}.$ Thus MSE at most $\epsilon^2$ requires $h_L\le\epsilon$ and $N_L\ge2\epsilon^{-2}$. The finest-level work alone is therefore $N_Lh_L^{-1}\ge2\epsilon^{-3}$. This grows faster than $\epsilon^{-2}(\log\epsilon^{-1})^2$, so the claimed logarithmic bound fails without a positive correction-variance decay rate.
